results.title: CoreWeave Raised Prices by 25 Percent. Its Near-Term Computing Capacity Is Still Effectively Sold Out
highlights:
CoreWeave says its near-term AI computing capacity is effectively sold out. That announcement comes after it raised prices across its product lineup by roughly 25 percent in July.

Rival AI cloud provider Nebius said Wednesday that it could sell its entire 2027 capacity today on terms similar to its latest deals, but it is deliberately holding some back for immediate customer needs. According to the company, shorter contracts can often command even higher prices.

Customers are paying premiums for near-term computing power, new contracts are becoming more profitable, and even older generations of Nvidia GPUs—the chips used to train and run AI models—are still commanding strong prices years after newer chips arrive.

...

“Pricing is extremely strong on short term deals,” Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Vasu Kasibhotla told Inc. Wednesday. Nebius, he noted, is now citing roughly $40 million in annual contract value per megawatt of data center power for short-term capacity, “materially higher than the $10-15 million the market expected just a year ago.”

...

Nebius entered 2026 with baseline annual contract value of about $12 million per megawatt. Its second-quarter deals averaged more than $20 million. It now sees an opportunity to charge $40 million to $50 million per megawatt for three-to-six-month deals.

results.title: A GPU from 2020 just sold at full price through 2029 · Stacks
highlights:
Reporting second-quarter results on August 11, CoreWeave said it had signed a contract on NVIDIA's A100, a chip from 2020, that runs to 2029, at full price. In the same call it said it had raised rental prices across its lineup by about 25% in July.

That report notes the increase came in two layers. The 25% raised against demand is one, and a pass-through of higher hardware costs sits on top of it.

...

The A100 launched in May 2020. A contract running to 2029 is nine years from that date. Chief executive Mike Intrator said the deal was struck at full freight, meaning without a discount, and the finance chief said average selling prices on older generations are at or above where they sat a year ago. The same release put second-quarter revenue at $2.575 billion, up 112% from a year earlier, with $104 billion of contracted work not yet recognised as revenue. Active power rose by about 500 megawatts during the quarter to 1.5 gigawatts, and the year-end target was raised above 1.85 gigawatts. All of these figures are CoreWeave's own disclosures. Who signed the contract, and what the price actually is, were not made public.

...

This is why a single contract does not settle it. CoreWeave is paid by the hour to run other people's compute, so an older chip pays as long as it stays booked. Meta and Oracle are using the gear to train their own models. When a newer chip does more work on the same electricity, the older one can be cheaper left idle. The same chip in a different seat is worth a different amount. There is one thing to watch. If more companies follow Amazon and shorten the life, CoreWeave's contract stays a fact about the rental business. If more follow Meta and stretch it, the reading that old GPUs still carry a price gets stronger.

results.title: Nvidia Blackwell Prices Surge 48%, Forcing AI Firms to Ration Services
highlights:
Nvidia's Blackwell GPUs have seen a significant price increase of 48% within two months due to high demand and capacity constraints, compelling AI companies to limit their services. This development underscores the growing challenges in meeting the computational needs of advanced AI systems.

...

The price of Nvidia’s highly sought-after Blackwell GPUs has surged dramatically, rising from $2.75 to $4.08 per hour over the past two months. This 48% increase is largely driven by a constrained supply of GPU resources amid a surge in demand from AI firms deploying powerful, large-scale AI systems. The rise in prices reflects the growing computational needs as companies race to develop and scale agentic AI technologies. 

The shortage of computing power is causing ripple effects across the industry, with many companies now forced to ration their AI services. Smaller firms and startups, in particular, are struggling to compete for limited GPU resources, potentially stalling innovation in certain areas. Meanwhile, larger corporations with more resources may gain an advantage, further exacerbating the gap between industry players.

...

The sharp rise in GPU rental costs could slow down advancements in AI by limiting access to computational resources, particularly for smaller companies. This may lead to greater consolidation in the AI industry as well-funded firms gain a competitive edge. Supply chain and resource constraints could also push governments and private sectors to invest in alternative computing solutions.

results.title: Cloud GPU Pricing Comparison: AWS vs Azure vs GCP | nOps
highlights:
Cloud GPU pricing varies 3-20x across providers depending on commitment model, billing granularity, and utilization rates. AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud Platform (GCP) dominate enterprise AI infrastructure with H100, A100, and V100 instances priced between $1.95/GPU/hour (spot) and $12.29/GPU/hour (on-demand) as of August 2026. 

The critical insight most GPU pricing comparisons miss: sticker price is not real cost. At 5% utilization—common for development and early-stage training workloads—an AWS H100 instance with a $12.29/hour list price costs $245.80 per utilized GPU-hour, because 95% of reserved capacity sits idle. Egress charges ($0.08-$0.12/GB), storage for training data and model checkpoints ($0.02-$0.18/GB/month), and idle time between jobs drive total cost of ownership 30-80% above nominal GPU rates.

...

## Hyperscaler GPU Pricing Comparison Table (August 2026)

Because GPU instances bundle multiple accelerators, comparing full instance prices can obscure the underlying economics. The rates below for AWS vs Azure vs Google Cloud GPUpricing are normalized to per-GPU-hour.

| GPU Model | Provider | Instance Type | On-Demand (per GPU/hr) | Spot/Preemptible (per GPU/hr) | Commitment Discount |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| NVIDIA H100 SXM5 80GB | AWS | p5.48xlarge (8 GPUs) | $12.29 | $1.95-$2.50 | 1yr: 30%, 3yr: 50% |
| NVIDIA H100 SXM5 80GB | GCP | a3-highgpu-8g (8 GPUs) | $9.00-$11.50 | $2.10-$2.80 | 1yr: 37%, 3yr: 55% |
| NVIDIA H100 SXM5 80GB | Azure | ND H100 v5 (8 GPUs) | $12.25-$14.50 | N/A (Low Priority VMs) | 1yr: 38%, 3yr: 62% |
| NVIDIA A100 SXM4 80GB | AWS | p4d.24xlarge (8 GPUs) | $5.26 | $1.30-$1.80 | 1yr: 30%, 3yr: 50% |
| NVIDIA A100 SXM4 80GB | GCP | a2-ultragpu-8g (8 GPUs) | $4.05-$4.80 | $0.90-$1.20 | 1yr: 37%, 3yr: 55% |
| NVIDIA A100 SXM4 80GB | Azure | ND96amsr A100 v4 (8 GPUs) | $5.00-$6.20 | N/A | 1yr: 38%, 3yr: 62% |
| NVIDIA V100 SXM2 32GB | AWS | p3dn.24xlarge (8 GPUs) | $3.06 | $0.92-$1.20 | 1yr: 30%, 3yr: 50% |
| NVIDIA V100 SXM2 32GB | GCP | n1-highmem-96 + 8x V100 | $2.48-$3.10 | $0.74-$1.00 | 1yr: 37%, 3yr: 55% |
| NVIDIA V100 SXM2 32GB | Azure | NCv3 (8 GPUs) | $3.06-$3.68 | N/A | 1yr: 38%, 3yr: 62% |
| NVIDIA L40S 48GB | AWS | g6.48xlarge (8 GPUs) | $4.88 | $1.46-$1.95 | 1yr: 30%, 3yr: 50% |
| NVIDIA L40S 48GB | GCP | g2-standard-96 (8 GPUs) | $3.75-$4.50 | $1.12-$1.50 | 1yr: 37%, 3yr: 55% |
| NVIDIA L40S 48GB | Azure | NVadsA10 v5 (8 GPUs) | $4.50-$5.20 | N/A | 1yr: 38%, 3yr: 62% |

Rates are for U.S. East regions (AWS us-east-1, GCP us-central1, Azure East US). Regional variance ranges 10-25% higher in Asia-Pacific and Europe.

Key takeaways from the cloud GPU pricing comparison chart:

- GCP offers the lowest per-GPU on-demand rates for H100 cloud pricing ($9.00-$11.50/GPU/hr) and A100 ($4.05-$4.80/GPU/hr)
- AWS spot instances provide deepest discounts (84-90% off on-demand for H100 and A100)
- Azure lacks true spot pricing — Low Priority VMs offer shallow discounts (20-30% vs 60-84% on AWS/GCP)
- All three providers offer 50-62% savings on 3-year commitments, but lock you into capacity you may not need

...

### 1.

...

GPU instances bill for uptime, not utilization. A training job that runs 1 hour per day on an 8-GPU instance reserved 24/7 achieves 4% utilization. At AWS p5.48xlarge on-demand rates ($12.29/GPU/hr × 24 hours × 8 GPUs = $2,359.68/day), that single training hour costs $2,359.68 — an effective rate of $294.96 per utilized GPU-hour.

...

AWS and GCP bill GPU instances per second (60-second minimum). Azure bills per minute (1-minute minimum). This matters most for short-duration inference jobs and batch workloads that frequently start and stop instances.

...

### On-Demand: Predictable Costs, Zero Interruptions

On-Demand is the highest per-hour rate, with no upfront payment, and you pay only for hours used.

#### Use on-demand when:

- Training runs are critical and cannot tolerate interruptions. Final model training before production deployment, research deadline experiments, customer demos that must complete on schedule.
- Workload duration is under 24 hours. On-demand avoids commitment lock-in for one-off jobs. Spinning up 8x H100 for a 6-hour fine-tuning job costs $589 on-demand (8 GPUs × 6 hours × $12.29/GPU/hr). A 1-year reservation saves 30% but requires paying for 8,760 hours of capacity you won't use.
- Spot capacity is unavailable in your region. H100 spot availability in AWS us-east-1 fluctuates between 0-60% depending on time of day. When spot is exhausted, on-demand is the only option.

### Spot/Preemptible: 60-84% Savings, Interruption Risk

AWS Spot Instances and GCP Preemptible VMs offer 60-84% discounts on GPU instances by reclaiming capacity when hyperscaler demand increases. CloudZero documented that "spot and preemptible pricing can lower [H100 costs] to $1.95-$2.50 per GPU per hour on AWS and GCP" versus $9-$12 on-demand.

...

### Reserved Instances: 50-62% Savings, Capacity Lock-In

1-year and 3-year commitments reduce GPU instance costs 30-62% in exchange for paying upfront or committing to hourly usage.

#### Use reserved instances when:

- Training workload is continuous and predictable. Foundation model pretraining that runs 24/7 for months. Inference clusters serving production traffic with steady request rates.
- You can accurately forecast capacity needs 12-36 months ahead. Over-provisioning a 3-year commitment wastes money. Under-provisioning forces you to pay on-demand rates for overage.
- Spot interruptions are intolerable, but you want on-demand cost savings. Commitments provide on-demand reliability at 30-50% lower cost.

...

Neocloud GPU providers (RunPod, Lambda Labs, Vast.ai, Latitude.sh, SynpixCloud) offer H100 access starting at $0.42/hour — 87-97% cheaper than hyperscaler on-demand rates. Why the price gap?

...

Lowest on-demand rates are essential. GCP H100 instances cost $9.00-$11.50/GPU/hr versus $12.29/GPU/hr on AWS — a 23-27% savings. For teams that cannot use spot or commitments, GCP minimizes on-demand spend.

results.title: CoreWeave Grew Revenue 112% and Nebius Grew Revenue 514% in One Quarter. Neither Number Means Your GPU Rental Gets Cheaper. | Solo Operator Stack
highlights:
Nebius also disclosed something more interesting than the growth rate: the payback period on new capacity deals shortened to 1 year and 10 months, down from a historical

...

Here's the part that headline readers skip. A $104 billion backlog doesn't mean CoreWeave has $104 billion sitting around waiting to be spent on discounts. It means $104 billion of future revenue is already contracted, and the company is racing to build the power and floor space to deliver on those contracts. Nebius signed four AI cloud deals in Q2 that averaged over $1 billion in total contract value each, with yields of $20 million to $25 million per megawatt, up more than 30% from Q1 pricing on older-generation GPUs. Prices per unit of capacity went up during the same quarter that revenue went up 514%.

That combination, rising volume and rising unit price, only happens when demand is outrunning what a company can physically build. If neoclouds had spare capacity sitting idle, they'd be discounting it to fill it. Instead Nebius ran its first capacity auction and is now testing $40 million to $50 million per megawatt pricing on short-term deals, a straight-up premium tier for customers who need compute now and can't wait for the standard buildout timeline. That's not what a market with excess supply looks like.

...

If you're a solo operator or small team buying GPU time from a neocloud (CoreWeave, Nebius, Lambda, Crusoe, or any of the smaller players), the leverage in that relationship currently sits with the provider, and there's no evidence that's about to flip. These companies are pre-selling 2027 capacity to customers with billion-dollar contracts and investment-grade credit. If you're negotiating a monthly on-demand rate against that backdrop, you are not the priority customer, and you're not going to out-negotiate a hyperscaler-backed contract with $40 billion in commitments behind it (that's Nebius's own disclosed total customer commitment figure, not a made-up number).

The practical version of this: budget for GPU rental costs to stay flat or rise over the next two to three quarters, not fall. If your current provider quotes you a renewal at the same or a slightly higher rate than last year, that's not price gouging, it's consistent with what both companies are telling their own shareholders about deal economics. Where you do have leverage is in commitment length and workload flexibility. Shorter, spot-style workloads are getting priced at a premium right now because that's exactly the capacity neoclouds are keeping scarce on purpose. If you can commit to a longer window or run less time-sensitive batch jobs, you're closer to the pricing tier hyperscalers get, not the one desperate short-term buyers get.

results.title: an interesting perspective from the founder of Jarvis.ai. | Ram Balasubramanian
highlights:
**Reshared from Vishnu Subramanian:**
> Nvidia announced $500B in financing platforms for AI factories yesterday, with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR. Most of the reactions I read were about circular financing and whether this is a bubble.
>
> Running a GPU cloud for the last six years gives me a slightly different view of this news.
>
> Two years back, there was so much supply that providers were competing by cutting H100 prices. Over the last year the trend has reversed. Our on-demand H100 is at $2.69 an hour today, 20 to 30% higher than a year back. Availability has gone down, customers want longer commitments, and people who need clusters instantly often pay more than the on-demand price. For the last six months, demand has been more than what we could supply.
>
> So the asset is holding value. What I don't see discussed much is what it takes to generate returns from it. Renting bare metal is where every GPU cloud starts, and it becomes a commodity quickly. The real work is everything above it: loading a large model in two to three minutes instead of ten, cold-starting containers in 1.8 seconds, routing traffic so the same GPUs serve more customers, keeping inventory busy across time zones.
>
> I wrote about this in more detail here: https://lnkd.in/g4rwh67T

results.title: CoreWeave verhoogt prijzen met 25 procent | FLOH Solutions
highlights:
CoreWeave verhoogde in juli alle SKU-prijzen met ongeveer 25 procent en meldt dat de capaciteit voor de korte termijn uitverkocht is. Ook oudere GPU-generaties worden niet goedkoper meer.

...

## Kort samengevat

- CoreWeave voerde in juli 2026 een prijsverhoging van ongeveer 25 procent door over al zijn SKU's, bevestigde CFO Nitin Agrawal op de kwartaalcall van 11 augustus.
- De capaciteit voor de korte termijn is volgens topman Michael Intrator feitelijk uitverkocht, ook voor oudere Nvidia-generaties; een pas getekend A100-contract loopt door tot in 2029.
- De verhoging raakt nieuwe contracten en verlengingen, niet de prijs van een lopend meerjarig take-or-pay-contract.
- Het is de tweede verhoging in twee maanden bij een grote aanbieder, na de circa 20 procent die AWS per 1 juli 2026 doorvoerde op zijn gereserveerde GPU-blokken.

CoreWeave verhoogde in juli de prijzen van zijn hele productlijn met ongeveer 25 procent, zei financieel directeur Nitin Agrawal dinsdag op de kwartaalcall, terwijl de capaciteit voor de korte termijn uitverkocht blijft.

Wie in Nederland AI-rekenkracht inhuurt, krijgt daarmee de tweede verhoging binnen twee maanden voor de kiezen. AWS trok de tarieven van zijn gereserveerde Nvidia-GPU-blokken per 1 juli al met ongeveer 20 procent omhoog, en CoreWeave gaat er in dezelfde maand overheen. Het tarief is niet het enige dat verandert. De klassieke uitwijk bij dure rekenkracht, een generatie oudere GPU's huren voor minder geld, is bij deze aanbieder dicht.

...

De stap raakt de SKU's: de losse producttypes in het aanbod, telkens een bepaald GPU-type met de opslag, het netwerk en de software eromheen. Agrawal zei dat de margeverbetering van het tweede kwartaal nog van vóór de aanpassing dateert, en dat die aanpassing een verhoging van ongeveer 25 procent over alle SKU's inhield. Als reden noemde hij de vraag in de markt en het rendement dat klanten op hun eigen AI-toepassingen zien nu ze verschuiven van trainen naar inferentie. Gestegen componentprijzen rekent het bedrijf daar bovenop door.

Een lopend contract verandert er niet door. CoreWeave verkoopt capaciteit vooral via meerjarige take-or-pay-afspraken, en die prijs staat vast voor de looptijd. De 25 procent landt op nieuwe contracten en op verlengingen. Volgens Agrawal komt er dit jaar maar een klein deel van de vloot vrij voor herverhuur, maar liggen de gemiddelde verkoopprijzen daarvoor op of boven het niveau van een jaar geleden. De contracten die het bedrijf in het tweede kwartaal tekende, dus nog vóór de verhoging, hadden al een bijdragemarge die 5 tot 10 procentpunt hoger lag dan die van recente kwartalen.

...

Topman Michael Intrator zei op dezelfde call dat de prijzen voor de nieuwste Blackwell- en Vera Rubin-generaties records neerzetten, en dat de tarieven voor eerdere generaties op of boven het niveau van jaren geleden liggen. Ook van die oudere generaties is CoreWeave naar eigen zeggen grotendeels uitverkocht. Als voorbeeld noemde Intrator een pas getekend contract voor A100-capaciteit dat doorloopt tot in 2029. Die architectuur stamt uit 2020.

Dat is het deel dat een inkoper meteen raakt. De rekensom "neem een generatie terug en betaal minder" ging jarenlang op. Nu houden ook oudere Nvidia-chips hun prijs, jaren nadat er nieuwere zijn verschenen, constateert Inc. op basis van de cijfers van CoreWeave en concurrent Nebius. Draai je een werklast die prima op een H100 of A100 past, dan koop je daarmee geen korting meer, maar vooral beschikbaarheid.

...

De verhoging landt in een markt waarin de klant weinig te kiezen heeft. Intrator zei dat de capaciteit voor de korte termijn feitelijk is uitverkocht, waardoor het bedrijf contracten op steeds gunstiger voorwaarden kan sluiten. Beleggers lazen dat als kracht: het aandeel steeg woensdag ruim 19 procent. Voor elke GPU die in gebruik wordt genomen melden zich volgens de directie meerdere klanten, en de capaciteit gaat bewust naar de contracten die CoreWeave strategisch belangrijk vindt.

results.title: Nebius Earnings: GPU Spot Prices Triple and Neoclouds Exploit Short-Term Scarcity | Morningstar
highlights:
Our key takeaways from Nebius Group’s NBIS second-quarter call are that GPU spot rental rates continue to climb as the artificial intelligence supply/demand imbalance intensifies and neoclouds want to maximize value extracted from short-term pricing.

Why it matters: Average contract value per megawatt has more than tripled in the year to date, from an average of $12 million/MW in early 2026 to $20 million/MW in the second quarter, and some third-quarter contracts are being signed at $40 million/MW. We think management is avoiding long-term capacity commitments, favoring three-to-six-month contracts, as it believes GPU spot rates will continue to climb, allowing a massive pricing tailwind in late 2026 and 2027.

- Quarterly revenue grew 454% to $582 million with a negative 30% operating margin. We estimate higher-priced contracts will have a significant positive impact on profitability in late 2026 and 2027. This massive pricing tailwind is supply/demand driven, not driven by any durable differentiation, and we remain cautious about assuming such pricing persists into perpetuity. Once the imbalance eases, the pricing situation would play in reverse.

The bottom line: We raise our fair value estimate for no-moat Nebius to $150 from $120, reflecting higher GPU rental prices in the next three years, improving operating margins, and reducing the free cash flow burn. We estimate Nebius will burn close to $30 billion in free cash flow in the next five years, requiring continued equity and debt raises.

results.title: GPU rental rates keep rising! | Ivana Delevska
highlights:
GPU rental rates keep rising!

Nebius and CoreWeave just reported earnings, and the biggest takeaway is simple:

AI compute pricing is going up — not down.

Despite enormous amounts of new capacity coming online, demand continues to outpace supply and contract economics are improving.

Nebius

▪️ Mid-term deals (1–3 years) are being signed at $20–25M per MW, or roughly $4.50/hr for GB300s, with prepayments covering 50–60% of capex.

▪️ Short-duration deals (<6 months) are clearing at $40–50M per MW, or roughly $9/hr — sometimes even higher.

▪️ Its first capacity auction cleared 15% above the highest price Nebius had ever charged for Blackwell. Management says it could sell all of its 2027 capacity today at current terms, but is deliberately holding some back because it expects better economics from near-term demand.

CoreWeave

▪️ Implemented a ~25% price increase in July, driven by scarce capacity and improving customer ROI.

▪️ New 2Q contracts carried contribution margins 5–10 points higher than contracts signed in prior quarters.

▪️ And this is happening while CoreWeave rapidly expands supply: active power grew 50% QoQ to 1.5GW, with contracted power already at 4.2GW in early Q3.

The conventional bear case has been that massive GPU deployments will eventually commoditize compute and push rental prices down.

So far, we're seeing the opposite:

More capacity. Higher prices. Better contract economics.

For neoclouds, that's a pretty powerful combination.
